title: Blue Solutions and AVL test solid-state battery safety - electrive.com
content:
Blue Solutions and AVL have completed a joint development programme to assess the safety of a new generation of solid-state batteries. The work focused on cell behaviour under high stress, preventing thermal propagation and preparing the technology for series production.
Image: Blue Solutions
French solid-state battery developer Blue Solutions and Austrian engineering specialist AVL have completed a joint safety assessment of Blue Solutions’ next-generation battery cells. The programme focused on identifying and mitigating potential risks ahead of the technology’s industrial-scale production.
To support the assessment, the partners combined Blue Solutions’ cell technology with AVL’s simulation, testing and validation expertise. The programme examined cell behaviour under increasing internal pressure, mechanical stability, and a range of stress and failure scenarios.
Blue Solutions’ next-generation solid-state battery uses a lithium-metal anode, among other new technologies. Compared with today’s lithium-ion cells, this cell design promises higher energy density but also introduces new engineering challenges, particularly in managing internal cell pressure and designing the mechanical structure of the overall battery system.
A key focus of the programme was thermal propagation, the spread of a thermal event from a defective or overheated cell to neighbouring cells. In the worst case, such a failure can trigger a chain reaction throughout the battery pack. According to Blue Solutions and AVL, the programme demonstrated that this risk can be reduced through simulation-based development, pressure-optimised cell design and a safety-oriented battery system architecture.
The partners said the simulation and validation results were positive and consistent. According to the joint announcement, the technology complies with key requirements of China’s mandatory GB 38031-2020 battery safety standard. The regulation defines safety requirements for traction batteries used in electric vehicles and includes testing at the cell, battery pack and system levels.
“Working with Blue Solutions’ latest solid-state battery technology is a significant step forward for AVL,” said Paul Schiffbänker, Director of Battery Development at AVL. “It not only deepens our understanding of the specific safety characteristics of this next-generation chemistry, but also actively drives the further development of our safety methodologies and battery design solutions.”
At the same time, the partners aim to preserve the cells’ high energy density. Blue Solutions and AVL are targeting a volumetric energy density up to 25 per cent higher than comparable battery packs based on NMC lithium-ion cells, allowing more energy to be stored within the same installation space. They also expect gravimetric energy density, which measures energy storage relative to battery weight, to improve by 13 per cent.
“From advanced simulation-based prediction models to new validation and assessment approaches, this collaboration enables us to systematically embed safety into the development of future high-energy battery systems from the very beginning,” Schiffbänker added.
Olivier Caumont, Battery Systems Director at Blue Solutions, sees the programme as confirmation of the concept’s market readiness. “[AVL’s] vision and mastery in multiple sectors, combined with our extensive manufacturing experience in solid-state batteries manufacturing and pack integration, including the safety, thermal or mechanical aspects, has enabled us to confirm that our solution is fully aligned with market needs and capable of fulfilling the most stringent safety requirements.”
Blue Solutions is currently developing the fourth generation of its solid-state battery technology. The company is already working with several partners to evaluate potential applications and plans to commercialise the technology for passenger cars by the end of the decade. The findings from the joint safety programme will be presented at international conferences and battery industry events.

title: China makes EV battery health more transparent - electrive.com
content:
China aims to set new standards for transparency in electric vehicle battery health with its voluntary GB/T 46991.1-2025 norm and has published new details. For example, display errors are to be limited to a maximum of five percent.
BYD Blade Battery (symbolic image)
Image: BYD
With the publication of details from the national standard GB/T 46991.1-2025, China is taking a significant step towards greater market transparency in the field of electric mobility. Led by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the Standardisation Administration of China (SAC), the standard defines binding measurement methods and reference values for the ageing of traction batteries in electric vehicles. The aim is to drastically reduce the discrepancy between the values displayed in the cockpit and the actual usable capacity.
The standard was published on 31 December 2025 and entered into force on 1 July 2026. It defines requirements and test procedures for assessing battery ageing, residual capacity and the reliable display of traction battery health.
A key element of the standard is the introduction of the State of Available Energy (SOCE). This metric compares the battery’s remaining available energy with its original condition, providing an indication of long-term capacity retention. Under the standard, the deviation between the SOCE value displayed in the vehicle and the physically measured value must not exceed five per cent. For the first time, this establishes a precise benchmark for battery health displays, clearly distinguishing SOCE from the short-term State of Charge (SOC). The metric indicates how much of the battery’s original usable capacity has been retained over time.
To ensure long-term battery quality, the standard also defines minimum SOCE thresholds based on vehicle age and mileage. Electric vehicles must retain at least 82 per cent of their original available energy after five years or 100,000 kilometres. The minimum threshold falls to 75 per cent after eight years or 160,000 kilometres, and to 70 per cent after ten years or 200,000 kilometres.
The standard also introduces the concept of virtual kilometres to account for energy consumed outside normal driving. Electricity used while the vehicle is stationary, such as for air conditioning or auxiliary systems, is converted into an equivalent driving distance. Here, too, the standard sets a strict accuracy requirement, limiting the deviation between the displayed and measured value to no more than three per cent.
The regulatory framework was developed under the technical leadership of an expert group headed by Yu Yang. According to the expert group, the new standard is intended to significantly improve transparency for consumers by making battery ageing measurable using standardised and traceable methods. It is also expected to reduce uncertainty about battery condition in everyday use and strengthen confidence in electric vehicles.
Although the regulation has initially been introduced as a recommended national standard rather than a mandatory requirement, it is expected to have significant commercial implications. In particular, the standardised battery health metrics provide a more reliable basis for assessing used electric vehicles. Industry observers expect the new requirements to influence residual value calculations, warranty claims and manufacturers’ product strategies.
China distinguishes between recommended national standards (GB/T) and mandatory standards (GB). While compliance with GB/T standards is voluntary, they often become de facto industry benchmarks. Manufacturers that do not align with MIIT-backed recommendations risk disadvantages such as reduced access to state subsidies, fleet procurement programmes or consumer confidence.

title: How are DHL and Vinted Growing Sustainable Ecommerce?
content:
How are DHL and Vinted Growing Sustainable Ecommerce?
Prioritise Us
on Google
Vinted and DHL are expanding their partnership in Germany. Credit: DHL
With consumer demand for more sustainable operations growing alongside re-selling, DHL and Vinted are expanding operations and making shipping easier
Consumer patterns are changing, which means organisations need to change with them. Logistics companies in particular have had to adapt to the increasing demand of ecommerce and online marketplaces.
Now, consumers expect fast and traceable delivery, flexible pick-ups and drop-offs and reliability. Alongside this, more consumers have began re-selling their items, breathing new life into unwanted clothes, shoes, bags and more.
As a result, organisations are working to meet consumers where they are at, which is why DHL and
are expanding their logistics cooperation.
Reselling used goods online has evolved from a niche activity to an everyday phenomenon within just a few years.
Benjamin Rasch, Head of Sales and Products, Post & Parcel Germany, DHL Group
Sustainability in fashion
The fashion industry has changed, driven by higher costs, less available income and a desire to be more eco-conscious. Fast fashion, though still a hearty market, is pushed aside for a new market: reselling. Following the boom of fast fashion from 2000 to 2015, where clothing production doubled, sales increased but utilisation decreased, circularity has become more of a priority.
Young people are making use of thrift stores and charity shops more, looking for that rare gem hidden between the rails. Alongside this, resale, rental and repair is becoming more of a focus, with more brands offering these services to their customers. Brands like Urban Outfitters and
Patagonia
offer upcycling capabilities for their customers, whereas M&S has a clothing resale partnership with eBay to offer its clothes another life.
Now, customers are wanting clothes that last, or they are more conscious about the impact of clothing waste. Alongside this greater awareness of waste reduction comes a more strict approach to spend – with the rise of inflation, consumers have less free spend available, meaning they are considering their money more than ever.
As a result, consumers have become more savvy, turning to online platforms to resell their items – clearing their wardrobe and receiving money at the same time, without contributing to clothing waste.
Fast fashion encourages high consumption and disposal rates, leading to significant environmental and social consequences. Credit: Temu
The rise of the marketplace
The rise of platforms such as Facebook Marketplace, Vinted, Depop and the
revival of eBay
has mean that trade is still flowing – big retailers are just less involved. According to research from Barclays, 19% of consumers are using platforms like Vinted in order to revive their wardrobe while keeping costs down.
Barclays finds that 38% of UK customers have purchased an item from a resale platform in the past year. Vinted now has more than 17 million users in the UK alone. As a result, the global second-hand market is valued at US$210-$220bn, with an annual growth of 10%.
This increase in reselling, however, means that logistics organisations are operating differently. In order to ensure the second-hand market continues to grow, DHL and Vinted have expanded their partnership in Germany. The latest DHL Ecommerce trends report revealed that 67% of online shoppers in Germany have already sold items using an online marketplace, making it one of Europe's most active markets for trade between individuals.
To support this, the two companies are bringing in their individual expertise – Vinted's platform reach as one of Europe's largest peer-to-peer second-hand marketplaces, and DHL's nationwide parcel service network. Through DHL's
vast locker network
, the companies are aiming to make shipping and collection more straightforward.
"Reselling used goods online has evolved from a niche activity to an everyday phenomenon within just a few years. As a result, expectations regarding shipping are rising. People buying and selling privately want shipping to involve as little effort as possible," explains Benjamin Rasch, Head of Sales and Products for Post & Parcel Germany at DHL Group.
Benjamin Rasch, Head of Sales and Products, Post & Parcel Germany, DHL Group
"It should be just as easy as purchasing from an online store. Many people want to send or collect parcels independently of opening hours. This is exactly why automated solutions such as Packstations are becoming increasingly important. That is also why we will continue to invest heavily in expanding our automated network in the years ahead. Vinted is one of the companies driving Europe's booming second-hand market. We are delighted to continue Vinted's success story in Germany together."
The logistics company already operates 41,000 parcel drop-off and collection points across Germany, which includes parcel shops, automated facilities and post offices. Its locker network is expected to grow from 18,500 to more than 30,000 locations by 2030.
The re-sale market
The global second-hand market is valued at US$210-US$220bn
The market is growing 3x faster than the firsthand market
One in four 16-24 year olds use resale platforms to save money
Approximately 25% of all UK fashion transactions are second-hand
Integrating flexibility
The peer-to-peer market place already relies on shipping services, with parcel lockers being a useful tool for those wanting to resell their clothes or purchase them. According to the DHL Ecommerce report, approximately 70% of respondents use automated lockers or parcel shops to ship their items, whereas only 30% hand over goods in person.
"Tons of people in Germany use Vinted to give products a second life. This requires shipping solutions that fit
seamlessly into everyday life
," explains Dovilė Riškutė, Senior Director of Business Development and Operations, Vinted Go.
Dovilė Riškutė, Senior Director of Business Development and Operations, Vinted Go
"Thanks to DHL's nationwide network and, in particular, its 24/7 accessible Packstations, our members can send and receive parcels with maximum flexibility. This provides a strong base for further expanding our offering in Germany, and deliver against our ambitious growth aspiration."
For many users of these platforms, having flexible postage and delivery options is crucial – allowing them to take care of logistics outside of working hours, at times which suit them.
DHL and Vinted's partnership is helping consumers shop more responsibly, with a greater focus on sustainability. Buying second-hand and trading
pre-loved goods
helps keep the products in use longer, with more opportunities for upcycling, rather than sending these goods to a landfill.
A core element of Vinted's business model is about keeping products in use and reducing the environmental impact of the fashion industry. The partnership focuses on resale and increasing access to low-emission logistics, as DHL operates more than 38,500 electric delivery vehicles in Germany alone.
Through the partnership, the companies are helping consumers shop more responsibly and revamp their closets in an economic way.

title: PepsiCo Impact: Supporting Jobs Across the US Supply Chain
content:
PepsiCo Impact: Supporting Jobs Across the US Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
More than 61,000 jobs are supported in the trade and transportation industry through PepsiCo. Credit: PepsiCo
PepsiCo has released a report exploring its impact on the US economy, as well as its interconnected job production across the nation's supply chain
PepsiCo has published a report, detailing its impact on the US economy and how the organisation is supporting thousands of jobs across America.
Using data from 2024 – the most recent full year of verified data – and an analysis from Oxford Economics,
PepsiCo explores how its footprint
extends further than its immediate workforce.
Around the world, supply chains are becoming bigger and more intricate, as global organisations expand their logistics networks, supplier bases and more. In its report, PepsiCo explores this, looking at the interconnected systems behind its US supply chain.
Key numbers
PepsiCo supports nearly 440,000 jobs across the US
The company contributes approximately 0.22% to the US's total economic output
PepsiCo has achieved 58% water replenishment
More than US$35.7bn in income was generate for American workers in 2024
Supporting job growth
Across its global portfolio, PepsiCo owns more than 500 brands, 23 of which generate more than US$1bn each in annual retail sales. Its products are sold in more than 200 countries and territories around the world, with brands including Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos and Pepsi-Cola. In 2025, it had a net revenue of almost US$94bn.
Around the world, it directly employs approximately 318,000 people, but its impact supports
thousands more jobs
In its latest impact report, using data from 2024, PepsiCo reveals that it supports nearly 440,000 jobs in the US alone. This includes people it directly employs (144,500 in 2024), as well as the people that work across its supplier base, logistics organisations, packaging companies and more. PepsiCo has a major reach across industries, supply chains and communities across America.
The report found that approximately two additional jobs were supported across the US economy for every person it directly employed. The company has generated job opportunities and economic growth across key sectors, including manufacturing (176,000), agriculture (14,500) and
trade and transportation
(61,800).
"PepsiCo’s impact and scale reflect how deeply our business is intertwined with the US economy and daily American life,” explains Steven Williams, PepsiCo Executive Vice President and Vice Chairman.
Steven Williams, Executive Vice President and Vice Chairman at PepsiCo (Credit: PepsiCo)
“From agriculture and manufacturing to transportation and food services, our operations support livelihoods and contribute to economic strength in communities across the country, while our products continue to provide enjoyment and choice for consumers.”
The economic impact
In 2024, the company contributed approximately US$64.88bn to the US GDP, which made up roughly 0.22% of the total economic output of the country. For workers, it generated more than US$35.7bn in income.
Some states gained more economic benefits than others, with a local GDP impact exceeding US$1bn in 22 states. This was even larger in some states, including Texas (US$8.1bn), Illinois (US$4.4bn) and New York (US$4.5bn).
Of the total GDP, US$30.27bn of it was generated for the manufacturing industry. Across the sectors, PepsiCo's GDP impact also includes:
Trade and Transportation (US$7.47bn)
Information and Professional Services (US$7.4bn)
Finance, Insurance and Real Estate (US$7bn)
Accommodation and Food Services (US1.3bn)
Agriculture
(US$1.8bn).
Across the entire supply chain, PepsiCo is supporting a range of industries – many of which are not often thought about in conjunction with the brand. Agriculture, manufacturing and trade are all known parts of the supply chain – the food must be grown, the product needs to be manufactured and then it needs to be shipped to its store.
However, a supply chain has much larger complexities, with a range of industries doing their part to help meet consumer demand. Through a range of outsourced functions, PepsiCo is driving economic success and job expansion across the US.
Thousands of jobs across the US are supported through PepsiCo. Credit: PepsiCo
Steven Williams, PepsiCo Executive Vice President and Vice Chairman
Developing supply chain resilience
As well as contributing to the GDP and the job market, PepsiCo is also working on driving long-term resilience across its broader supply chain, using sustainability measures and social impact efforts to drive change. The company has an end-to-end transformation strategy, aiming to protect natural resources and empower communities.
Around the world, PepsiCo is working directly with farmers to expand capabilities in
regenerative agriculture
, restorative and protective practises. As of 2025, it has made an impact across 4.7 million acres, helping develop more resilience and improve farmer livelihoods. Through working on regenerative agriculture processes, farmers can make long-lasting changes to their operations, helping them become more self-sufficient and
more sustainable
As of 2025, PepsiCo has achieved 100% water replenishment in its facilities which are in high water-risk areas. Across the US and the wider world, almost 29 billion litres have been restored to local watersheds. Its dedication to protecting and preserving natural resources is helping produce new jobs and more resilience across the supply chain. Through this, the organisation is protecting its operations and the communities it operates in.

title: Apple & Broadcom: A Strong US Supply Chain Agreement
content:
Apple & Broadcom: A Strong US Supply Chain Agreement
Prioritise Us
on Google
Some of Apple's logic boards and advanced AI servers are produced and assembled in Houston, Texas. Credit: Apple
Apple is investing further in its US supply chain following a US$30bn deal with Broadcom for a multi-year chip agreement
Apple has committed
to purchasing more than 15 billion custom chips from Broadcom under a multi-year deal agreement valued at more than US$30bn. The arrangement forms part of Apple's American Manufacturing Program and represents one of the largest supplier commitments the company has made for custom silicon components.
According to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Broadcom entered into new long-term agreements to develop and supply custom ASIC silicon products. The contracts extend prior arrangements between the two companies, including a 2023 deal for 5G radio frequency components and FBAR filters.
Apple designs its own application processors and has worked to internalise modem development. However, the company continues to rely on Broadcom for custom radio frequency chips that connect devices to cellular networks.
Capacity planning and manufacturing investment
The multi-year commitment covers design and production of custom silicon components and wireless connectivity technologies. According to Apple, the agreement will enable Broadcom to expand and modernise manufacturing facilities in Fort Collins, Colorado with a US$1.5bn investment.
The Fort Collins site handles production of radio frequency components that Apple previously designated for manufacture in what it called "several key
American manufacturing
and technology hubs". Broadcom wireless products first appeared in Apple devices in 2009 with the iPhone 3GS, which used a chip combining Wi-Fi and Bluetooth features.
Tim Cook, Apple's CEO, said the companies have "a long history together" and that the new phase of the partnership "further accelerates our commitment to American manufacturing and innovation". He added that components built in Fort Collins are "essential to delivering the incredible performance and connectivity our customers expect".
Tim Cook, CEO of Apple. Credit: Apple
Tim said Apple is "proud to deepen our investments in US-based suppliers that share our commitment to excellence and innovation". He thanked the president and his administration "for supporting important projects like this one".
Manufacturing strategy and policy considerations
In May 2025, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that he had "long ago informed Tim Cook of Apple that I expect their iPhone's that will be sold in the United States of America will be manufactured and built in the United States, not India, or anyplace else". Trump said that if this requirement is not met, "a Tariff of at least 25% must be paid by Apple to the US".
That same year, Apple announced its American Manufacturing Program, an investment of US$600bn in
US manufacturing.
The company plans to hire 20,000 people in the US under this programme, with the majority in roles focused on R&D, silicon engineering, software development and AI and machine learning.
According to Apple's second quarter FY2026 earnings call, Cook discussed how the company is "advancing American supply chain innovation", including work on an end-to-end silicon
supply chain
across the US. He said Apple is "on track to purchase well over 100 million advanced chips" from TSMC's Arizona facility.
In Peoria, Arizona, near the TSMC plant, Apple is investing in an advanced chip packaging and testing facility operated by Amkor. The American Manufacturing Program supports tool installations at Texas Instruments' facility in Lehi, Utah and a new facility in Sherman, Texas.
Broadcom has signed a multi-year chip supply deal with Apple. Credit: Apple
Supply constraints and demand planning
Tim said Apple has been facing supply issues for several products, including iPhones and Mac products such as the Mac Studio and Mac mini. He attributed this to "higher than expected demand", in part due to customers recognising the potential of these devices for "AI and agentic tools".
The constraints could show the challenges of matching production capacity to demand forecasts in markets where new applications create consumption patterns. Apple's procurement strategy appears to address these risks through long-term supplier agreements that secure component availability.
Many components Apple purchases from Broadcom are US-made, which could insulate it from geopolitical risks, tariffs and shipping bottlenecks. The domestic manufacturing footprint provides
supply chain resilience
compared to components sourced from other regions.
Supplier relationships and foundry partnerships
While Broadcom operates its own fabrication facilities for technologies such as RF filters, the majority of its high-volume digital and logic silicon is manufactured by partners including TSMC and GlobalFoundries. By committing early and for extended periods, Apple secures its supply of Broadcom components regardless of where those components are ultimately fabricated.
Outside of Broadcom, most of Apple's in-house-designed silicon is made by TSMC. The volume of chips Apple purchases makes it a notable customer, which could give it priority access to the company's manufacturing capacity.
According to PwC, global semiconductor
chip demand
will grow at a compound annual growth rate of 8.6% to 14.8% through 2030. In March, Taiwan's Economic Daily reported that TSMC is fully booked until 2028.
While Apple already maintains a relationship with TSMC and has previously sourced specific silicon from Broadcom, the new commitment could provide the opportunity to proxy-book further TSMC capacity. This approach could further insulate Apple from industry-wide chip supply issues by securing foundry capacity through its component suppliers.

title: Volvo's next electric SUV will start in the upper $40,000 range
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 3 2026 - 8:49 am PT
is preparing to launch the EX50 in the US, an entry-level electric SUV aimed at the Tesla Model Y that will start at under $50,000.
When is Volvo launching the EX50?
Following the EX60, Volvo is already preparing to introduce its next electric SUV. The EX50 is set to arrive at dealerships in 2027, replacing the EX40 as Volvo’s most affordable electric vehicle in the US.
Sources familiar with the matter told
Automotive News
that the EX50 is taller and longer than the EX40.
It will also be slightly cheaper, starting in the upper $40,000 range compared to the 2026 Volvo EX40, which starts at $56,545.
After reporting second-quarter earnings last month, Volvo said it would unveil two new electric models by the end of Summer. The same week, it
filed a trademark
for the EX50 name with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO).
While the filing didn’t reveal much outside of the name itself, the EX50 will be based on the new SPA3 platform, the same one that underpins the EX60.
2027 Volvo EX60 (Source: Volvo)
The 800-volt platform delivers faster charging, a longer driving range, and more interior space. It’s also flexible enough to support a wide range of body types and different battery pack sizes.
Volvo will build the new electric SUV, codenamed V326, at its manufacturing plant in Kosice, Slovakia.
Volvo EX60 interior (Source: Volvo)
It will arrive in 2027 in an increasingly crowded segment that’s still dominated by the Tesla Model Y. Volvo’s entry-level electric SUV will be closer in size to the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Toyota bZ, and Ford Mustang Mach-E, which are among the best-selling EVs in the US.
Some Volvo dealers are already getting excited. Matthew Haiken, owner of Prestige Volvo in East Hanover, NJ, said the EX50 is much like the Polestar 7, which will also be built at the plant in Slovakia.
Volvo EX40 (Source: Volvo)
Haiken, who had to stop selling Polestar vehicles in the US, said having a Polestar-like model to offer is “both exciting and a little disappointing.”
“At least I know Volvo will get a competitive product that gives us real differentiation from Tesla,” he said, adding “and hopefully a sliver of their market share.”
Electrek’s Take
Volvo has struggled to sell electric cars in the US with the Trump Administration’s policy changes, including import tariffs and the loss of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit.
In the second quarter, Volvo’s fully electric vehicle sales fell 44% with just over 1,500 models sold. The EX40, based on its old CMA platform, is due for an update, but it appears Volvo will introduce an all-new vehicle with the EX50.
Will it help compete in the US? Outside of the Tesla Model 3, the
top 10 best-selling EVs
in the US were electric SUVs in the first half of the year.
The Model Y remained in first by a wide margin, followed by the Model 3, Hyundai IONIQ 5, Toyota bZ, and Chevy Equinox EV.
Starting under $50,000 with fast charging, at least 300 miles of range, and modern tech, the EX50 may find its market in the US.

title: Tesla Model Y RWD 2026 Review: an entry-level trim with top-of-the-line technology
content:
Tesla Model Y
Bastien Theron
| Aug 3 2026 - 7:59 am PT
I drove the 2026 Model Y RWD (Standard) for about 550 km (342 miles) across a mix of highway, back roads, and city driving, and I enjoyed the efficiency and technology far more than the driving experience itself. For anyone shopping for an affordable Tesla built around the brand’s software and ecosystem, this standard trim is a real contender, but it drives more like a generic SUV than the brand promises.
Here is the full review:
Abstract
The 2026 Tesla Model Y RWD (Standard) I tested is the Canadian-market LFP version, rated for 463 km (288 miles) of range at 7.3 km/kWh (4.6 mi/kWh), that’s
136.4 Wh/km (219.6 Wh/mi)
, an efficiency figure I matched almost exactly over roughly 550 km (342 miles) of highway, backroad, and city driving.
Charging held up well too, with a 10-80% Supercharger session completed in 24 minutes, and the LFP chemistry adds a genuine bonus: V2X discharge of more than 12 kW without worrying for battery degradation. Acceleration is the trade-off; at 7.2 seconds 0-100 km/h, it’s the slowest Tesla yet.
2026 Tesla Model Y RWD (Standard)
Storage is a genuine strength, with a spacious frunk, a deep subfloor trunk bin, and a nice open center console. It is fitted with one of the best user interfaces I have tested, even without a dedicated driver screen. The trade-offs of the Standard trim show up elsewhere: windows isolation is basic without double-paned, the closed roof feels cramped, and the 7-speaker sound system is a real disappointment coming from other Teslas.
Dynamically, this is the least Tesla-like Tesla I have driven; handling feels closer to a generic SUV than to the precise, planted feel I associate with the brand, and the blended brake-by-wire pedal takes some getting used to.
Driver assistance more than makes up for it: FSD (supervised) remains the best point-to-point
system available in North America, though it comes at a $99 monthly subscription, with
Autosteer
(lane-centering) no longer offered outside of it.
Overall, this standard trim’s $ 39,990 USD ($ 49,990 CAD) price undercuts the Premium by $ 6,000 USD, or $ 15,000 CAD, but it strips out meaningful equipment, from the panoramic roof’s opacity to the missing tow package.
It’s not quite the affordable EV breakthrough Tesla once promised, but for buyers who value the software and efficiency over outright driving dynamics, it remains a compelling entry point into the Model Y lineup.

For the 2026 model year of the base Model Y, Tesla offers 2 different battery packs depending on where the vehicle is built. For the
, with the vehicle built in Fremont or Austin, it is fitted with a
battery, smaller than the Premium trim (~80kWh) but composed of the same NCA cells in fewer numbers. They removed some of the paralleled cells and manage to reduce the energy capacity while keeping the same number of cells in series and so the same
max voltage. This new battery pack would be a 96S40P architecture, instead of the 96S46P of the Premium trim.
Elsewhere in the world, meaning a Y produced in Shanghai or Berlin, the Y RWD is fitted with an
battery pack of about
. Living in Canada, this is the vehicle I was able to test drive as we cannot get our Teslas from the US, even if that would make the most sense logistically and environmentally, thanks to dumb tariffs.
The battery pack engineering being weighted in this category, the score will reflect the vehicle I drove, equipped with the LFP battery, which is a nice upgrade in technology, bringing a much longer life out of the pack, the ability to daily charge to 100% without second thought on the battery degradation, and great charging performance. It is a nice upgrade over an NCA or NMC battery pack for the same energy capacity. It is not, however, the best LFP battery out there, far from BYD and CATL’s current generation.
If I were to review the US vehicle, my appreciation in this category would be lower, as the pack is an alternate version of aging 2017 technology. It was the best pack at the time, but nearly 10 years later, very few upgrades were made and charging performance actually decreased. Fortunately, 3 & Y energy efficiency has improved tremendously over the past decade, making up for the lack of battery improvements.
However, with the LFP version I got to drive, the improvements in the powertrain are added to battery improvement, resulting in quite a nice package.
Speaking of powertrain, this Model Y is equipped with a brand-new motor and drive combo, its only one, mounted on the rear axle. It is an evolution of the motor introduced in 2017 with the Model 3, with a redesigned rotor, stator and inverter for a lighter and more efficient powertrain, and I must say it is quite impressive for its efficiency.
More on that in the next category
It is nice to see Tesla still improving its vehicle powertrains, especially since its powertrains are already at the top and it could become complacent, as it did with its batteries.
A welcome addition, even nicer with an LFP battery pack with a cycle life so much longer than the vehicle, is the possibility to discharge the battery through a V2X (vehicle-to-everything) system at powers in excess of 12kW (I personally reached 14kW) without the vehicle’s ECU throwing an error. This means, with the proper home installation, you are not buying just a vehicle, but also a backup battery of ~60kWh for your home. This feature also works with other trims of the Model Y, so the US Model Y RWD should have it too, and
I hope it will not be removed
Discharging the Model Y to power my house
Electric Performance & Charging
(17.1 / 20)
The Model Y RWD (Standard) I drove is rated for an amazing efficiency of just 7.3 km/kWh (4.6 mi/kWh), that’s
136.4 Wh/km (219.6 Wh/mi)
, for a total range of
463 km (288 miles)
. During my few days with it I achieved an average of 7.4 km/kWh (4.6 mi/kWh), that’s
135.9 Wh/km (218.6 Wh/mi)
, on my ~550 km (342 miles) road test, composed of mostly highway and backroads, meeting th eofficial efficiency.
On back roads only, at an average speed of 78 km/h (48 mph), it achieved an efficiency of 8.0 km/kWh (5.0 mi/kWh), that’s 124.7 Wh/km (200.7 Wh/mi), on a 140 km (87 mile) trip. That’s more than impressive considering the size and weight of it! Otherwise, I’m pleased to report the rated efficiency can be achieved while driving normally, or at least with my driving style as it is not the case for all the vehicle I review.
The best efficiency I achieved during a real commuting
The efficiency I achieved during my ~550km with it
The 2026 Model Y RWD is as efficient as the 2026 Model 3 RWD, while being bigger, and it’s thanks to the new powertrain Tesla is debuting. I’m crossing fingers for this powertrain to make the jump into the Model 3 next.
The LFP battery pack is limited to 175kW of peak charging power, or 2.77C, but since it held it for a while and can maintain more than 100kW (1.58C) at 65%, my 10-80% charging test result in 24min on a Supercharger V2 capped at 143kW, for an average charging power of 110kW or 1.75C. This is a very good result, in line with what I want to see from a new EV, and I
a full 0-80% charging session on Supercharger V3 at 175kW to last the same 24min at an average charging power of exactly 2C, or in other words capable of charging up to 370 km (230 miles) in 24min.
Supercharging capped at 143kW on a V2
The charging performance of the US model is
expected
to follow those of the Premium trim which are at an average of about 32min for a 0-80% resulting in an average charging power of 103kW or 1.5C, and based on the EPA rating, it is good for a range of 516 km (321 miles), which means, in 32 minutes, up to 412 km (256 miles) can be recharged.
Acceleration is the Model Y RWD’s weak point, making it the slowest Tesla yet. At 7.2s 0-100km/h, it’s far from bringing the “Tesla Smile” when pressing the throttle at standstill. I think the power delivery is clearly limited by software, as the amount of power and torque available from a standstill feels noticeably less than at around 40 mph (64 km/h) while cruising. My guess is this is a software lock meant to create a gap between the Standard and Premium models, even though I suspect both are running the same motor and drivetrain hardware.
Ergonomics, Cabin & Storage
(16.2 / 20)
Cabin refinement is decent, if not flawless for an entry trim vehicle. Materials used are nice to touch, and the minimalist approach looks clean. Maybe a little too much for some.
Minimalist design with great view
The only mechanical buttons are on the steering wheel
Driver & passenger textile-vegan leather seats
View from the 2nd row. There is a Glass roof behind this fabric trim
All 3 adjustable headrests for the 2nd row
Road noise Isolation is excellent, and cabin noise in general is low at 66db. However, wind noise creeps in at the windows, most likely because this Model Y skips double-pane glass, and the closed roof, while giving the black trim a clean look, makes the cabin feel more cramped than I’d like. Climate control, on the other hand, is good and intuitive, as with any Tesla, and you can even option oscillating vents that swing the airflow for both the driver and the passenger, which is a first for me, and I liked that feature. You have to get used to doing everything on the display though.
Seats are average, with fabric upholstery that keeps them from getting too hot, though ventilation isn’t offered, only heating and only for the front row.
Storage is an area where the Model Y shines. It has plenty of storage in the cabin with a minimalist central console, resulting in quite a bit of open space, which I actually enjoy as it allows fitting multiple items, and bigger ones too, compared to the closed central console we’re used to.
Open space in the center floor
Central Console with USB C inside
The trunk, with its electric opening even for a low-cost trim, is more than adequate for this category of vehicle, with 2 deep pockets on each side behind the rear wheels, as well as a subfloor bin competition should take note of. Added to that tremendous amount of storage is a frunk which I find quite useful when going somewhere for 2 days with the wife, toddler and dog; stroller and dog in the trunk, luggage in the trunk’s subfloor bin and both pockets and groceries in the frunk.
A lot of space in this trunk
The underfloor storage is so useful!
With the 2nd row flatten
Frunk, without sealing when closed.
For this standard trim of the Model Y, strangely enough, the frunk isn’t sealed, so you get to select which type of luggage you use it for, depending on the weather. Also worth noting, the hood is made of steel instead of aluminum on other trims. Tesla states they do this for cost-cutting, though I do not think they have enough volume of this part, since it’s only for the entry trim, to make it actually cheaper than the aluminum one used on about a million vehicles a year. It’s a bummer for those living up north, as steel hoods tend to be pitted by the sand/salt on the road and are prone to corrode, whereas aluminum will last longer.
Wireless charging for 2 phones also sits in a convenient spot for the driver and passengers, not blocking anything and working well in our tests. Unlike with my Cybertruck, I could charge my iPhone 14 Pro with sufficient power on this wireless charging pad without any temperature derating; however, it’s not the fastest wireless phone charger I’ve tried. Yes, my phone heats up, but not enough to cancel the charge, which, for me, is the baseline for a wireless phone charger.
Wireless phone charger right below the display
One more minor gripe: there’s no auto-dimming for the side mirrors, like in most low-cost vehicles; you’ll be blinded at night by the reflection from the following vehicle’s headlight. I know some drivers don’t like auto-dimming mirrors; that’s not the case for me!
Unlike other Teslas, the charge port door on this Model Y doesn’t open when you press the button on the charger handle; you have to open it by touching it, or via the phone app or the vehicle UI. It’s a small inconsistency to find on a car built on the same platform as the rest of the line-up.
NACS charging port, obviously
Software & User Interface
For the first time, seat controls live on the screen rather than as physical buttons on the seats themselves, and honestly, it works fine for me; I rarely adjust my seat while driving anyway, maybe during the first few minutes to find my ideal position, and after that I never touch it again. However, if you are one of those who constantly adjust your seat while driving,
this is not for you
; you will find it cumbersome unless you rely heavily on FSD (supervised), more on that later.
Both seats adjustments controls live on the display
The steering wheel has to be adjusted manually. Mirors are adjusted on the display like every Teslas
Speaking of the screen, the UI is one of the best I tried. You have to get used to having only one center screen and no information or instrument cluster behind the wheel; something that I got used to quickly to the point that I find most integration of screens by other manufacturers to be dumb, as way too often the instrument cluster behind the steering wheel isn’t visible in its entirety… thanks to the steering wheel in front of it! So, no screen behind the steering wheel is a good solution in my opinion.
Then there’s the UI’s actual layout and capabilities; the screen is divided into two sections, with about a third on the left used mostly for vehicle-mandatory information such as speed, flashers, and headlights indication, power output (I’d like to have actual numbers instead of just a progressive bar), battery state of charge and trip meters. The rest of the screen will be used by the navigation. On the bottom of the screen, there is a menu bar, with access to the HVAC system, controls/parameters of the vehicle, quick access to the seat controls, and the application drawer. Up to 6 applications can be added to the bar for quick access.
Speaking of the applications, the Model Y, like all Teslas, doesn’t disappoint. You’ll find an Energy app to track your efficiency, a web browser, streaming apps such as Netflix, games, goodies, music streaming platforms, Zoom, a calendar synced to your phone’s, and others. When you open an app, it will be layered over the navigation, with critical navigation information moving to the left side of the screen for the driver’s attention.
Main layout
HVAC Settings
HVAC rear activation
Applications drawer
Dash Cam Player
Energy App / Trip meter
Energy App prediction over reality
Calendar App
Camera App (Front and side)
Camera App (Rearand side)
Vehicle Controls
Available Audio App
Service options
There is no Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and frankly it’s not necessary. Everything responds super fast and is clear and easy to understand. You can play around with the navigation, dragging and panning as you would on your phone, with the same sensitivity. It remains, hands down, one of the best infotainment systems on the market.
Only the stalk is present on the left side of the steering wheel, only for the turn signals; everything else is controlled from the wheel or screen, which takes some getting used to. That’s a recurring issue with Tesla: there can be three different wheel-button configurations across the line-up, which is a bit of a nuisance. I don’t mind it myself, though, but it’s worth trying before deciding whether it works for you.
Onboarding is great, with plenty of useful information shown on the central screen to help configure the car. I’ve been driving Teslas for the last eight years, though, so I’m probably not the best judge of whether it’s good or bad for someone completely new to the brand.
Interactive onboarding
Driving Experience
(10.1 / 15)
The driving feeling is where the Model Y RWD (Standard) disappointed me. Driving it felt more like driving a standard low-cost SUV than a Tesla, at least dynamically. For me, Teslas are about precision in handling and acceleration, which you won’t find with this trim of the Model Y.
Suspensions are comfortable though, and isolation from the road is pretty good. However, the rear end gets a bit bouncy and overall handling feels so-so; the car doesn’t feel very planted on the road. Whether that comes down to suspension tuning or the tires remains to be investigated. The handling felt more like a generic SUV, something that may appeal to the majority of buyers, after all, those vehicles are the most sold on the planet; it’s just a shame the Model Y RWD (Standard) doesn’t manage to distinguish itself here.
The main process I dislike on this vehicle is the blend of regenerative and hydraulic braking on the brake pedal. It felt to me the first few inches of travel simply activate the switch that brings on regeneration, and after that you get the hydraulic power, which is quite firm underfoot, thanks to a brake-by-wire design. Anyone who has a racing simulator at home, such as a Logitech G923 with a game such as Forza, will understand the feeling; it’s working the same way in the vehicle, the brake pedal is just mounted on a strong spring and sensor. As you push it, it sends a signal to the braking system, which applies hydraulic pressure to the braking system. This way isn’t new; many vehicles have used it for years. For the Model Y, it could have been implemented better in my opinion. I recommend you try it for yourself and see if you like it. I might be picky, but for me, the brake pedal should be hydraulic-only, with an option to add more regen either via a button behind the steering wheel, as GM does, or as a menu setting. I prefer keeping everything under the control of my right foot, on the throttle, for a precise one-pedal driving experience, and I don’t like how this blended brake pedal feels.
The sound system is a real disappointment. It sounds muffled, heavy on bass, and light on mids, to the point that I can’t hear voices properly; that’s the biggest downgrade on this vehicle by far, coming from the excellent sound systems in the Premium Model Y, Model 3, or Cybertruck. If you care about sound quality, this is not for you. Even the old standard speaker set available on previous Model Y generations was better in my opinion. That said, most people probably don’t pay much attention to it, and even as-is, it still beats listening through your phone, laptop, or tablet, so it makes sense on a low-cost model.
A recurring topic in my reviews is the ease of road-tripping, and the Model Y technology doesn’t disappoint. Thanks to the quick and reliable charging, amazing efficiency, a wonderful ADAS (more on that in the next category), and the best User Interface I’ve tested, with a nearly flawless navigation system, road trips are no-brainers.
You can easily enter a destination in the Navigation system, and it will calculate the number of charging stops required, based on real-world data such as elevation, speed, and weather conditions. It will also show the waiting time at each charger, and you can add stops or preferred locations to go through to reach your end destination.
There is a level of voice-enabled commands you can use for the navigation, if you like this sort of thing.
The battery will be preconditioned on the route to a fast charger, as long as it is set in the navigation. Preconditioning works all the time when navigating to a Supercharger and most of the time when going to another charging network.
Navigation with trip planning
On a positive, even this base trim of the Model Y offers the Auto-Shift feature that automatically shifts forward or backward depending on the surroundings and the driver’s inputs. It is a feature I like much more than having to shift gears on the touchscreen, since there is no stalk or button for it. Shifting into gear using the touchscreen is okay most of the time, except during a 3-point turn. Thankfully, this Auto-Shift feature can take care of that.
Shifter on the left edge of the display, you have to swipe it up or down
The Model Y RWD (Standard) is a genuinely capable SUV, with plenty of storage, an okay range, and room to fit 5 adults. Unfortunately, there is no official towing package for this trim, so an upgrade to the Premium trim is required.
Driver Assistance Systems
(9.1 / 10)
ADAS on this Model Y is genuinely impressive. It is one of the best driver-assistance systems available at this price point.
Level 2 ADAS
, Tesla’s FSD (Supervised) is the best system available in North America, also currently the only point-to-point Level 2 system. You can literally get in your car, fasten your seat belt, then start FSD (Supervised) and enjoy the ride. Don’t forget to input your destination into the navigation, or you are in for a surprise random destination.
The system will handle stop signs, traffic lights, and all the necessities to drive on public roads. It is an Advanced Driver Assistant System, though, and you have to pay attention to what it does and be ready to take over at any time. It
make mistakes.
ADAS Configuration
ADAS Configuration
ADAS Configuration
Lane following is working nearly flawlessly, even on poorly marked or unmarked roads, such as snow or gravel. Speed control and acceleration from standstill are very comfortable, reducing the possible motion sickness.
During my testing, there were two areas of improvement. The first is the vehicle’s parking space selection. It tried multiple times to use a disability parking spot or a forbidden parking spot. For a
system, though, it’s a minor discomfort.
The second area for improvement is speed limit sign recognition and compliance. Unfortunately, the system does not recognize a new speed limit, resulting in the vehicle going either too slow for the new allowed speed limit or too fast, depending on the sequence of speed limit signs. At other times, specifically in rural areas where the speed limit is 50km/h, the system can completely ignore the limit and go more than 25 km/h over it.
It is to be understood that there are 5 different profiles for the system, all impacting the speed and acceleration targets. Sloth, Chill, Standard, Hurry, and Mad Max. All of my testing was done on the Standard profile, which most resembles my driving style, with about +10km/h over the speed limit and quick enough accelerations without discomfort. However, there is no way to set a hard speed limit that could result in a ticket, for which you, the driver, would be responsible.
Generally, this ADAS works so well that you might be tempted not to pay attention to the road, which could be a fatal mistake. It is amazing, I would say, 98% of the time, but you need to be alert to the other 2% when it messes up. I like it a lot, though, as it drives very smoothly and feels natural and effortless.
Auto parking at destination
Auto parking copleted
Interpretation of the surrounding by the ADAS system
That’s for when you are paying the required
$99 a month
for the system. If you don’t, you only have access to the active safety features (Lane departure assist/avoidance, Blind spot monitoring, rear cross traffic alert, Auto Emergency Braking, Forward collision warning) and Traffic Aware Cruise Control, which is Tesla’s version of adaptive cruise control. Autosteer, or lane centering, isn’t available anymore outside of FSD (supervised); I do not like that.
Autosteer coupled to TACC is what we called Autopilot in the past, and removing it is a real downgrade for new owners as not everyone finds value yet in a point-to-point system like FSD (supervised), and this system needs you to pay a subscription which feels wrong to me when owning a vehicle where the hardware is present regardless.
For this category, I’ve reviewed the vehicle as I tested it, so with FSD (supervised) enabled, on Quebec’s roads. Without it, the score would be way lower at 4/10 since only the active safety features and TACC would be present.
Extra is a category Teslas naturally fall into; they were the first to bring real goodies and entertainment to a car, and the Model Y RWD (Standard) doesn’t take any of it away.
The Toy Box alone is worth exploring; there’s a sketch pad, which my two-year-old daughter loves, along with the option to have the car’s on-screen model rendered as a Tron Light Cycle or Santa’s sleigh, and no shortage of easter eggs to find along the way.
Toy Box App
Streaming is built right into the UI, with YouTube and Netflix natively supported. There’s also a full internet browser, which I’ve found genuinely useful for road-tripping, whether I’m looking up a place to visit or checking its opening hours. The same browser can also play full-screen video and audio, so you can pull up Prime Video, Disney+, or whatever streaming service you prefer; video is locked to only play while the vehicle is parked, of course.
Youtube runs natively
On top of all that, there’s a solid line-up of games available directly on the car, such as Stardew Valley, Beach Buggy Racing, and Fallout Shelter, to name a few.
Quite a lot of games are available for when you are waiting
(6.8 / 10)
The perceived value of the Model Y RWD (Standard) is where it gets dicey. And it’s different in the US versus in Canada. Below is a list of all the features removed from the premium trim, for a decrease of $6,000USD in the US to $39,990USD and $15,000CAD in Canada for $49,990CAD:
Performance & Range, the only category with differences between the countries
(US Only) 0-60 mph drops from 5.4s to 6.8s
(US Only) Battery capacity is trimmed to 69 kWh, down from 78.1 kWh on the Premium version, dropping range to 321 mi (516 km) vs 357 mi (575 km) on Premium
(Canada Only) RWD vs AWD since the Premium RWD trim isn’t offered
(Canada Only) 0-100 km/h drops from 4.8s to 7.2s
(Canada Only) Battery capacity is trimmed to 63 kWh, down from 78.1 kWh on the Premium version, dropping range to 463 km (288 miles) vs 542 km (337 miles) on Premium
(Both) Charging power is downgraded to 175kW peak, down from 250kW on Premium
Exterior
19-inch aluminium wheels are swapped for basic 18-inch steel wheels with plastic wheel coverings
Front and rear LED light bars are removed, replaced with redesigned single-unit headlights that lack adaptive Matrix high-beam function but Auto High-beam is present.
Headlights are dimmer and illuminate closer to the vehicle than the Premium. It is acceptable though, comparable to other base vehicles.
Manual folding only and no auto-dimming side mirrors
Ride & comfort
Passive cheaper suspension replaces the more advanced shocks found on Premium
Regular particulate filter instead of a HEPA filter
Simple 7-speaker setup, with no FM radio instead of the amazing 15-speaker system with subwoofers
Interior/Seats
Dual-tone vegan leather/cloth mix with only front seats heating versus the full vegan leather heated seats front and rear, and ventilated front seats.
Rear seats fold manually instead of power-folding
No positioning buttons on the front seats, done in the screen instead.
The rear 8-inch touchscreen for climate/entertainment controls is missing
The rear center armrest is removed entirely, and the rear cupholder access requires folding down the middle seat
Rear cup holder requires folding the middle seat
The panoramic glass roof is retained physically, but fully covered with an opaque fabric headliner so it’s no longer see-through
Other reported omissions
No frunk isolation and drain plug
No interior jacket hooks
No Towing package available at the manufacturer level
No response of the charging port door to the button click of the handle
That said, what isn’t compromised at all is the technology and the top-of-the-line UI experience. It is running exactly the same software as any other Tesla, without any hidden or locked features.
2026 Model Y RWD Front view
2026 Model Y RWD side view
2026 Model Y RWD rear view
I’ll let you be the judge of whether the price decrease relative to the premium trim makes sense for you. For tech-oriented people, where UI and software are highly valued, the Model Y RWD (Standard) is highly valuable. For those who don’t care about software and are more about the driving experience, it’s going to be a hard sell, and I recommend going with the premium trim.
Compared with competitors’ base trims, the Model Y RWD (Standard) falls in the middle of the pack in price while offering an arguably better UI and ecosystem, and similar driving performance.
I must admit I do not understand the choice to block the glass roof with fabric. It cannot be cheaper than leaving the glass roof as is, since it is installed anyway. Other than differentiating the standard trim from the premium one, I don’t see the point. Tesla could have offered a nicer vehicle, for the same entry price point, and it would have cost them less money to keep the glass roof visible.
Unfortunately, it isn’t priced at the entry models for the masses we were expecting, or even promised, which tints the score in this category. Getting it below $35,000 USD in the US and $42,000 CAD in Canada would have been a game changer for mass EV adoption.
In Canada, though, the pricing is another story. While it fits in the middle of the pack against direct competitors, you can currently get a Model 3 with nearly all the premium features, except for the sound system, for $39,490 CAD (~$28,000 USD), cheaper than the base stripped Model 3 in the US, which is priced at $36,990 US, thanks to the ability to import vehicles from China into Canada. While this Standard Model Y asks for a noticeably higher price, it offers far fewer features and that math doesn’t quite add up. I hope Tesla will replace the current Model Y RWD (Standard) offering in Canada, which is made in Berlin, with a Premium RWD version from Shanghai for a similar price to the Model 3, at around $ 45,000 CAD. That would sell like hot cakes! As it stands right now, potential buyers in Canada had better be locked into owning an SUV as you can get a much better vehicle for cheaper if you can sacrifice on the storage and ease of entering the vehicle.
Finishing on this topic, having to subscribe for $99 a month to get FSD (supervised), with no option for purchase, isn’t great. It means you could lose the feature if the company went under, much like we are seeing with digital media purchases, such as games and movies, or, most likely, the price will trend upward as the take rate increases, having you pay more and more for your vehicle. I really don’t like that. Moreover, the hardware is already on the vehicle, so either you have already paid for it or Tesla is losing money when people do not subscribe. Since the majority of buyers aren’t subscribing yet, I’m more inclined to think the first.
I get it: the software needs constant work to improve, and they have to find a way to pass that cost on to the customer, but instead of going the full SAAS way, I would prefer to have a base version of the system included with the purchase of the vehicle and then pay for a significant update. This way, if you are perfectly happy with the system, you don’t need to pay more money, you actually own something physically, and you have the freedom to choose.  Even the previous model, where you could choose between a full purchase of the system for a hefty price or a subscription-only option, was better than today’s. You had freedom of choice. I’m concerned about this trend of manufacturers pushing more subscriptions into everyday products, and I do not see the competition coming in to undercut that and bring better products for less money, as it should be in a healthy market.
One word on the mandatory servicing of this vehicle: I like that Tesla is basically stating, “don’t service it unless you need to” for most parts.
Maintenance summary
Fitness for Purpose
As an SUV, the Model Y RWD (Standard) fits its purpose with plenty of storage, good EV capabilities, and seating for 5 adults. The only miss is towing capability, which Tesla doesn’t offer on this trim. The Premium trim can tow up to 3,500 lbs; it would have been nice to get some towing capacity on the entry model too, since they share the same frame and powertrain.
As the game-changing affordable EV it was supposed to be, it doesn’t quite deliver on that promise; instead, we’re left with a middle-of-the-pack-priced SUV, which is disappointing.
Safety is where this Model Y earns its perfect score, with little debate. NHTSA gives the 2026 Model Y a five-star overall rating, with five stars in every individual assessment as well.
This version is also the first vehicle to pass NHTSA’s newly updated advanced-driver-assistance testing, clearing the bar for pedestrian automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assistance, blind-spot warning, and blind-spot intervention, all of which come standard.
The IIHS hasn’t published its own results for the 2026 model yet, but between the federal testing and the standard active-safety suite, it’s hard to find much to fault here. Moreover, Euro NCAP rated the refreshed Model Y from 2025 as the Best in Class in its safety tests.
Electrek’s take
I was skeptical of this version of the Model Y. Since we were expecting a new entry-level model with a really low price point, I was disappointed when the Model Y Standard was first unveiled (before being named Model Y RWD). However, I must say after testing it and comparing it to the competition, I now think Tesla brought something compelling to the market.
To appreciate it, you need to forget what you know about the handling capabilities and joy of driving of a Tesla and instead approach it as a vehicle for newcomers to the brand. The impeccable software ecosystem and UI will be of great value to tech enthusiasts who have never experienced them before, and the price of this trim is competitive compared with equivalent feature sets. I am very impressed by the efficiency, a testament to the fact that Tesla hasn’t stopped innovating on that front and won’t lose its crown without a fight. Energy efficiency is one of my main interests and too few manufacturers are giving it thought.
There are some things I find dumb, like the glass roof covering and the switch from aluminum to steel for the hood. Removing the frunk seal isn’t ideal either, as it limits its usefulness. I would have removed the electric trunk door opening before this seal.
Also, I personally don’t like the brake pedal feel and behavior in this vehicle at all. There are some people who like it though, so try it, you might be one of them.
I would have liked the acceleration to be a little better; targeting 6.5s from a 0-100km/h instead of 7.2s would make a big difference and put this vehicle more in line with the brand while still remaining the slowest Tesla.
I’ve owned a 2023 Model Y Dual Motor for 2 years, and comparing them, I can say the 2026 RWD (Standard) is quieter, more comfortable, and way more efficient, resulting in nearly the same real-world range and faster charging (with the LFP battery). However, Handling, acceleration, sound system, brake feeling, and towing capabilities sharply distinguish them.
Last thoughts: I dislike the driving experience of this trim of the Model Y, mostly because it drives like any other soulless SUV, but on every other metric it scored pretty well, earning it a nice overall score. This shows that my scoring system is more about technology and capabilities than about the subjectivity of experiencing a vehicle. Let me know if you’d like me to change the weighting of each category accordingly.

title: Tesla Supercharger shooting sparks EV charging safety debate
content:
Fred Lambert
| Aug 3 2026 - 7:30 am PT
After a gunman opened fire at a Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out with an attached Tesla Supercharger last week, EV owners flooded social media with the same suggestion: buy an EVject.
The breakaway charging connector lets you drive off while still plugged in. It sounds like an obvious fix for a horrifying scenario — but it’s a controversial device that doesn’t actually solve the problem, and it points to something Tesla and every other automaker should be building instead.
What happened, and why it hit a nerve
On August 1, a shooter targeted the crowd outside a newly opened In-N-Out in Twin Falls. A Supercharger sits in the same lot, and video circulating online appeared to show the gunman firing into a Tesla that was plugged in and charging. Three people were killed and several injured, including a driver who was charging his Tesla and survived.
WATCH: Video reportedly shows one of the two believed suspects opening fire with what appears to be an AR-style rifle in a parking lot in Twin Falls, Idaho. No word on casualties.
The detail that set off EV owners is a real one: when a car is charging, you can’t just floor it and leave. The connector physically locks into the port while power is flowing. To go, you normally have to tap “unlock charge port” on the screen or use the manual release, then wait for the cable to disengage. In a situation where seconds matter, that’s a genuine vulnerability.
That’s the gap EVject fills. The $299 “Escape Connector” sits between the Supercharger cable and your port and is designed to break away when you drive off, so you can leave immediately without unplugging.
Right after the events of this weekend, hundreds of Tesla owners on X started to share the EVject device with referral codes to promote it as a solution to this tragic event.
The device Tesla tried to kill
Here’s the part the viral posts leave out: this is the same accessory
Tesla sued in 2024, calling it a safety risk
Tesla argued in a California court that the connector could reach dangerous temperatures — its filing claimed surface temperatures as high as 100°C after 30 minutes of high-current charging — and that there was no over-temperature protection in the design. EVject later released an updated version with built-in thermal protection, and Tesla dropped the suit.
So the product now being promoted as the answer to a shooting is a third-party adapter that Tesla itself was in court over less than two years ago. That doesn’t make it useless, but it’s a strange thing to recommend without the asterisk.
A device doesn’t make you safe
Even setting the controversy aside, EVject only helps if you recognize the danger and act on it in time.
That’s the harder truth about the Twin Falls situation. A breakaway connector assumes you have the seconds and the awareness to shift into drive and go. In a sudden, chaotic attack, the people in those cars almost certainly had little opportunity to process what was happening, let alone execute an escape maneuver. No accessory changes that.
A tool that shaves a few seconds off an escape is worth something. But selling it as the solution to random violence oversells what a $299 adapter can do, and it risks giving owners a false sense of security.
This isn’t a Tesla-only problem
It’s also worth being clear that this isn’t unique to Tesla.
The charging connector locks during a session on every EV. It’s a safety requirement baked into the
, CCS, and J1772 standards — the plug latches so it can’t be pulled out while high-voltage power is flowing, which prevents arcing and accidental disconnection. Any EV plugged into a DC fast charger has the same constraint. Tesla’s
Supercharger network
is just where most people encounter it because it’s the largest.
That’s exactly why the fix shouldn’t be an aftermarket band-aid.
Electrek’s Take
The real answer here is a native emergency disconnect, built into the vehicle, that works from the driver’s seat. Well, in fact, the real answer is more likely gun control and serious invesments into mental health, but that’s out of our scope of expertise.
Tesla is well positioned to do an in-car solution. It controls both the car and the charger, so it could safely cut power, release the latch, and let you drive away with a single deliberate action — the kind of thing you’d want gated behind a confirmation and maybe a fee to prevent abuse and cover any equipment damage. Owners have been asking for exactly this since the shooting, and it’s a reasonable ask. It would be far safer than a breakaway adapter that mechanically separates a live connector.
But this shouldn’t be a Tesla-only feature, and it shouldn’t require buying a gadget that the manufacturer once called a fire risk. Every automaker and charging network should be thinking about how a driver safely leaves a stall in an emergency. The locking connector exists for good engineering reasons, so the escape path has to be engineered too — by the people who build the cars and the chargers, not bolted on afterward.

title: Aniioki’s latest 6,000W dual-motor e-bike blurs past the line so much it’s basically an electric motorcycle
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Aug 3 2026 - 6:34 am PT
If there’s one trend that has defined the direct-to-consumer e-bike industry over the last few years, it’s the relentless race toward bigger numbers. Bigger batteries. Bigger motors. Higher top speeds. And now Aniioki has unveiled what may be one of the most extreme examples yet.
The company’s new
A9 Pro Max Dual Motor 2.0
arrives with up to 6,000 watts of peak motor power, a claimed top speed of well above 50 mph (80 km/h) depending on the version, and battery options topping out at a staggering 5 kWh. Those numbers go beyond just big e-bike figures and pass well into legitimate electric motorcycle numbers.
At first glance, the A9 looks like a fat tire e-bike. It has pedals, a bicycle saddle, and 26×4.8-inch tires. The
US $2,899 price tag
isn’t even that lofty by high-power electric bike standards. Look a bit closer, though, and it quickly becomes clear that this machine is playing an entirely different game.
And while you
pedal it, those massive motors and the tempting throttle mean that the pedals are likely to become a set of splayed footrests for most people.
Aniioki is offering the bike in three different configurations.
The entry-level 60V 2.0 version uses dual 2,500W motors (6,000W peak combined) and reaches claimed speeds of 40-45 mph (64-70 km/h).
Step up to the 60V 3.0 model and output increases to dual 3,000W motors (7,000W peak combined), bumping claimed top speed to 51-55 mph (82-88 km/h).
Then there’s the flagship 72V version, which retains the dual 3,000W motors but pairs them with a higher-voltage electrical system and 72V battery. That pushes claimed speeds to between 54-60 mph (87-98 km/h) while also increasing torque, controller output, and climbing ability.
Those battery packs deserve some attention of their own. The 60V models are available with either 70Ah (4,200 Wh) or 80Ah (4,800 Wh) batteries. For comparison, many commuter e-bikes today carry around 600-800 Wh. Even cargo bikes often struggle to break 1,000 Wh.
A 5 kWh battery is entering small electric motorcycle territory, and in fact does surpass the battery capacity of many
electric scooters
mini-motorcycles
Aniioki claims up to 200 miles (320 km) of pedal-assist range under ideal conditions, though like all range estimates, actual performance will depend heavily on speed, terrain, rider weight, and how much throttle versus pedaling is involved.
The company has also focused heavily on safety and durability, highlighting a 4 mm-thick aluminum battery enclosure, semi-solid blade battery cells, battery management system protections, and a patented frame claimed to be twice as strong as conventional bicycle frames while supporting riders up to 400 lb (180 kg).
Stopping power has also received considerable attention. The company uses CBS (combined braking system) paired with oversized 300 mm brake rotors. The flagship 72V model upgrades further with eight-piston front calipers and six-piston rear calipers, hardware more commonly associated with motorcycles than bicycles.
And speaking again of motorcycles, this is where we have to address the elephant in the room.
Yes, it has pedals.
But once you’re talking about 50-plus mph, 6-7 kW of motor power, and a battery larger than many electric motorcycles, calling something an “e-bike” becomes increasingly difficult to justify outside of marketing language. Of course, we have to remember that the term “e-bike” is largely colloquial and rarely exists in any legal frameworks. For example, even California, which has some of the more strict interpretations of the three-class system, never uses the term “e-bike”. The vehicle we’re all thinking of is legally known as an “electric bicycle”, which is why “e-bikes” have long been a catchall for everything from cute little 250W European electric bicycles to 80 kW high power electric motorcycles.
So the argument of whether or not this thing is an e-bike is somewhat moot. The real question is whether or not it’s an electric bicycle. And legally speaking, it’s not.
In most jurisdictions, this would not qualify as a legal electric bicycle under Class 1, 2, or 3 definitions. Those regulations typically cap assisted speeds at 20-28 mph and motor power around 750 watts in the US. Depending on where it’s operated, the
A9 Pro Max
is likely much more appropriately categorized as an electric moped or lightweight electric motorcycle.
That doesn’t mean machines like this shouldn’t exist. There’s clearly a growing market for riders who want something that sits between an e-bike and a full motorcycle. Sales are booming, and the dollars speak for themselves. But it does highlight an increasingly awkward reality in the industry: simply bolting pedals onto an electric motorcycle doesn’t automatically make it an electric bicycle – at least not as far as the law is concerned.

title: Argentina's solar train brings zero-emission travel to an ancient trade route
content:
Solar power
Electric train
Jo Borrás
| Aug 3 2026 - 5:04 am PT
The Tren Solar de la Quebrada is Latin America’s first primarily solar-powered passenger train, carrying tens of thousands of travelers through the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Quebrada de Humahuaca with the power of the sun.
El Tren Solar de la Quebrada celebrated its second anniversary last month, after ferrying passengers and eco-tourists through the Argentinian province of Jujuy on a 42 km (~26 mile) restored historic railway branch line that crossed the Quebrada de Humahuaca (Humahuaca Canyon).
UNESCO recognized the high canyon in 2003 for its cultural significance as a trade and migration corridor that’s been in constant use for more than 10,000 years
linking the people of the Andean highlands with the lowlands since prehistoric times
. Since its official launch last year, the solar train carried 90,000 passengers along that same route, connecting towns and boosting local economies without noise or emissions.
The train, itself
The train itself can ferry up to 388 passengers (72 seated) along the route, powered a 352 kWh li-ion battery pack that –
along with regenerative braking on downhill sections of its runs
– offers more than enough range to complete the ~52 mile round trip on a single charge. If the train ever
need to charge, each of the six stations currently on the route have EV-style chargers capable of “juicing it up,” with their power sourced from a dedicated 6 MW solar farm backed by stationary battery storage. In other words: there’s no combustion, anywhere.
As interesting as the train is
, though, its impact is much more significant than environmentally-conscious commuting.
“One of the defining characteristics of the project is its social impact,” reads the train’s official site. “Of the more than 90,000 passengers transported in the last two years, around a third traveled as part of the Solar Train’s social responsibility program. In other words, 1 in 3 passengers accessed the experience through initiatives aimed at bringing the train closer to the community.”
Phase 1 of the Tren Solar de la Quebrada currently runs between Volcán and Tilcara, but the project’s long-term vision includes extending the route north to Humahuaca and eventually La Quiaca, near the Bolivian border. There’s no published timeline for that future expansion as yet, but we are here for it.
